questions.q: Cell C2 contains the state growth rate (1.5%). You need a formula that multiplies prior year population by (1 + state rate) and can be dragged DOWN column G. Which reference to C2 works?
questions.explanation: Dragging down increments row unless locked. $C$2 locks both; C$2 locks just the row (enough here). Rule: $ before what must stay fixed.

questions.q: Dragging DOWN only (not right), you need D7 frozen and C4 to move with each row. Which formula?
questions.explanation: Freeze D7's row with D$7 (row locked, column free). Leave C4 bare so it becomes C5, C6, etc.

questions.q: Which reference locks both column AND row?
questions.explanation: Full absolute ($A$1) locks everything. $A1 locks column only, A$1 locks row only.

questions.q: F4 (or Fn+F4 on Mac) on a cell reference cycles through what?
questions.explanation: F4 rotates through the four dollar-sign combos. Fastest way to add absolute references without typing $.

questions.q: Which is a MIXED reference?
questions.explanation: Mixed = one part locked, one free. Both A$1 and $A1 are mixed.

questions.q: You're in F4 and enter =C2. You copy the cell to F6. What does F6 show?
questions.explanation: Relative refs shift by offset. F4→F6 is +2 rows, so C2→C4.

questions.q: You have =A$1+B1 in C1 and drag DOWN to C2. What does C2 become?
questions.explanation: A$1: row locked (doesn't change on down-drag). B1: fully relative, becomes B2.

questions.q: You have =A1+B1 in C1 and drag DOWN to C2. What does C2 become?
questions.explanation: Fully relative → both rows shift +1 on down-drag.

questions.q: Difference between COUNT and COUNTA?
choices: COUNT counts numbers only; COUNTA counts any non-empty cell
COUNT counts text; COUNTA counts numbers
questions.explanation: COUNT = numeric only. COUNTA = not empty (text or numbers). County names? COUNTA. Populations? COUNT.

questions.q: Which correctly sums A2:A40 where B equals "Metro"?
questions.explanation: SUMIF syntax: (range_to_test, criterion, sum_range). Test range FIRST, sum range LAST. Opposite of SUMIFS which has sum_range first.

questions.q: Count counties in B2:B40 with poverty > 15% (rates in C2:C40):
questions.explanation: Comparison criteria MUST be in quotes: ">15", "<>0", ">=100". Bare numbers can omit quotes.

questions.q: What does AVERAGEIF(A2:A40, "Metro", B2:B40) do?
choices: Averages A2:A40 where B is Metro
questions.explanation: Same (range, criterion, values) pattern as SUMIF.

questions.q: If you wrote =SUM(C7:C45)/SUM(D7:C45), what happens?
choices: Excel auto-corrects D7:C45 to C7:D45 (2-column block)
questions.explanation: Excel silently fixes inverted ranges into proper order. D7:C45 becomes C7:D45. The formula won't error, it will silently include an extra column — classic trap.

questions.q: A cell shows 0.347 and you want it to display 34.7%. Fastest?
questions.explanation: % format multiplies display by 100 and adds %, underlying value unchanged. Formulas referencing it still work.

questions.q: Find highest poverty rate in column C:
questions.explanation: MAX, not MAXIMUM. LARGE(range, k) exists but needs k.

questions.q: Difference between SUM(A1:A10) and SUM(A1,A10)?
questions.explanation: Colon = range. Comma = discrete cells. =SUM(A1:A10) sums all ten; =SUM(A1,A10) sums only A1+A10.

questions.q: State growth rate in C2. D3 needs to multiply C3 by (1 + state rate) and drag DOWN. Which works?
questions.explanation: C3 must shift with each row (leave bare). C2 must stay pinned ($C$2 or C$2).

questions.q: =COUNTIF(A2:A40, "Metro") counts what?
questions.explanation: COUNTIF counts matches. Case-insensitive by default.

questions.q: The & operator in =A1 & B1 does what?
questions.explanation: & joins strings. Same as CONCATENATE(A1, B1). For spaces: =A1 & " " & B1.

questions.q: SUMIFS argument order is:
questions.explanation: SUMIFS puts sum_range FIRST then pairs. This is OPPOSITE of SUMIF. Biggest SUMIF/SUMIFS trap.

questions.q: SUMIFS differs from SUMIF by:
questions.explanation: SUMIFS(sum_range, crit_range1, crit1, crit_range2, crit2, ...). Use for 2+ conditions. Similar: COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIFS.

questions.q: What does =TODAY() return?
questions.explanation: TODAY() = date only. NOW() = date + time. Both recalc on workbook open / any change.

questions.q: A1 = 2026-04-17. =YEAR(A1) returns?
questions.explanation: YEAR returns a number. Similarly MONTH (1-12) and DAY (1-31).

questions.q: Build a date for Dec 25, 2026:
questions.explanation: DATE(year, month, day). Order matters.

questions.q: Count days between date in A1 and today:
questions.explanation: Dates are serial numbers; subtraction works. DAYS(end, start) is explicit.

questions.q: A1="King", B1="County". =CONCATENATE(A1, " ", B1) returns?
questions.explanation: CONCATENATE joins with whatever you put between. " " is a literal space.

questions.q: =LEFT("King County", 4) returns?
questions.explanation: LEFT(text, n) = leftmost n chars. RIGHT = rightmost. MID(text, start, n) = middle.

questions.q: Which cleans "  King County  " (stray spaces)?
questions.explanation: TRIM removes leading/trailing spaces and collapses internal multi-spaces. CLEAN removes non-printable chars.

questions.q: =LEN("King County") returns?
questions.explanation: LEN counts every character including spaces: 4+1+6 = 11.

questions.q: =IF that returns "High" if A1>15 else "Low":
questions.explanation: IF(condition, if_true, if_false). Text needs quotes.

questions.q: Return "Metro" if pop>50000 AND unemployment<5, else "Other":
questions.explanation: AND() and OR() are functions, not keywords in comparisons.

questions.q: Grade nested IF: A≥90, B≥80, C≥70, else F (value in A1):
questions.explanation: Nested IFs: each ELSE slot is another IF. Test high threshold first. Modern alternative: =IFS(A1>=90,"A",A1>=80,"B",A1>=70,"C",TRUE,"F").

questions.q: VLOOKUP for A2 against table F2:H40, return 3rd column, EXACT match:
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP(value, table, col#, range_lookup). FALSE or 0 = exact match (use this 99% of the time).

questions.q: Key advantage of XLOOKUP over VLOOKUP:
choices: Can look LEFT (return col can be to left of lookup col)
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP only looks right. XLOOKUP works either direction, defaults to exact match, and has built-in not-found handling.

questions.q: XLOOKUP returns "Not Found" for missing values via:
questions.explanation: XLOOKUP has if_not_found: =XLOOKUP(A2, range, return, "Not Found"). IFNA also works.

questions.q: =IF(OR(A1="Metro", A1="Urban"), "Yes", "No") returns "Yes" when:
questions.explanation: OR() returns TRUE if ANY condition true. AND() requires ALL.

questions.q: Shortcut to convert range to Excel Table:
questions.explanation: Cmd+T on Mac, Ctrl+T on PC. Ctrl+L also works.

questions.q: Inside a Table named "Sales", reference the "Amount" column for CURRENT row:
questions.explanation: [@ColumnName] = current row. TableName[ColumnName] = entire column.

questions.q: Totals row on an Excel Table does what?
choices: Adds a row below with dropdown aggregations (Sum, Avg, Count, etc.) per column
questions.explanation: Each column in the totals row gets its own dropdown. Choose the aggregation. Excel remembers.

questions.q: You add a new row below an Excel Table. What happens?
choices: Table auto-expands to include the row, applies formatting/formulas
questions.explanation: Auto-expansion is the main reason Tables beat plain ranges.

questions.q: In a Table, you enter =[@Price]*[@Quantity] in the first row of an empty column. What happens?
choices: Formula auto-fills down the whole column
questions.explanation: Calculated columns auto-propagate. One of the killer features.

questions.q: OUTSIDE a table, =SUM(Sales[Amount]) does what?
choices: Sums entire Amount column, auto-updating as rows are added
questions.explanation: Structured refs outside: TableName[ColumnName] = whole column. Auto-expands. Use for dashboards.

questions.q: To make each region a separate row in a PivotTable, drag region to:
questions.explanation: Rows = unique values → row labels. Columns = unique values → column headers. Values = aggregations. Filters = pivot-wide scope.

questions.q: You drop Population into Values, it shows "Count of Population". You want Sum. How?
questions.explanation: Right-click any value field → Value Field Settings. Options: Sum, Count, Average, Max, Min, etc. Default for numeric fields is usually Sum; for text, Count.

questions.q: Grand Total: 39 on a pivot with region in Rows and Count of County in Values means:
questions.explanation: Grand Total = aggregation across all pivot values. 39 counties in Washington.

questions.q: A pivot shows South Puget Sound with "Count of County: 6". Means:
choices: 6 counties are classified as South Puget Sound
questions.explanation: Row label total = rows in source data matching that label.

questions.q: Pivot: region in Rows, Metro status in Columns, Count of County in Values. "Northeast / Metro = 3" means:
choices: 3 counties are BOTH Northeast AND Metro
questions.explanation: Row × Column intersection = records matching both conditions.

questions.q: To create a PivotTable:
choices: Insert → PivotTable → choose range → drop location
questions.explanation: Insert tab → PivotTable. Pick source range and target location.

questions.q: Region rows + Avg Unemployment values. "Southeast" shows highest value means:
choices: Highest average unemployment rate among Southeast counties
questions.explanation: Average aggregation scoped to row's records. Mean unemployment is highest among Southeast region counties.

questions.q: Source data updated. Pivot refreshes via:
questions.explanation: Pivots do NOT auto-refresh. Manual via right-click or ribbon button.

questions.q: Same Population field dropped to Values TWICE:
choices: Two Value fields appear — useful for Sum + Count side-by-side
questions.explanation: Multiple aggregations allowed. Drop same field twice, change one's aggregation, see both at once.

questions.q: Show population change over years (2017, 2018, 2019). Best chart:
questions.explanation: Line charts = trends over continuous intervals (time). Column works too. Pie is for parts of whole.

questions.q: Show each county's share of state total population. Best chart:
questions.explanation: Pie = share of whole, but unreadable with many slices. 39 counties → bar chart sorted.

questions.q: Check if two numeric variables are correlated:
questions.explanation: Scatter: X and Y both numeric. Shows relationships. Add trendline for regression.

questions.q: Compare populations across 10 counties with long names. Column vs bar?
questions.explanation: Horizontal bars give each label a full row width. Vertical columns cram/rotate labels.

questions.q: Change a chart's type after creation:
questions.explanation: Chart Design tab appears when chart selected. Change Chart Type swaps without losing data binding.

questions.q: Add axis labels and title:
questions.explanation: Add Chart Element menu: Titles, Axis Titles, Legend, Data Labels, Gridlines, Trendlines. Also + icon beside selected chart.

questions.q: 3D pie chart with 15 slices is:
questions.explanation: 3D distorts. >6 slices unreadable. Sorted bar chart is the pro move.

questions.q: Conditional formatting to highlight cells > 15000:
choices: Select → Home → Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Greater Than
questions.explanation: Home tab → Conditional Formatting menu. Built-in: Highlight Cells, Top/Bottom Rules, Data Bars, Color Scales, Icon Sets.

questions.q: Which conditional format shows a mini in-cell bar graph of relative magnitude?
questions.explanation: Data Bars = bar inside cell. Color Scales = gradient/heatmap. Icon Sets = categorical icons.

questions.q: Sort by Region (asc), then Population (desc within region):
questions.explanation: Custom Sort supports multi-level. Sort Region A→Z, Then by Population Largest→Smallest. Sorting twice does NOT work — second sort overrides first.

questions.q: Toggle AutoFilter dropdowns on selected data:
questions.explanation: Also under Data tab → Filter button.

questions.q: Filtered to only Metro counties. =SUM(A:A) of the range:
choices: Sums ALL including hidden — SUM ignores filters
questions.explanation: SUM ignores filter state. For visible-only, use SUBTOTAL or AGGREGATE.

questions.q: Function that sums only visible/filtered rows:
questions.explanation: SUBTOTAL(function_num, range). 9=SUM, 1=AVG, 3=COUNTA. Respects filters and hidden rows.

questions.q: Data Validation does what?
choices: Restricts what values can be entered (dropdowns, ranges, date ranges)
questions.explanation: Data → Data Validation. Types: List (dropdown), Whole number, Decimal, Date, Time, Text length, Custom.

questions.q: Create a dropdown cell with "Metro" or "Non-Metro" choices:
choices: Data → Data Validation → List → Source: Metro,Non-Metro
questions.explanation: Data Validation with Allow: List. Source can be comma-separated values or a range reference.

questions.q: Fill A2:A40 with sequential IDs 1-39. Fastest:
choices: Type 1 in A2, 2 in A3, select both, drag fill handle to A40
questions.explanation: Fill handle auto-detects series from 2+ cells. =ROW()-1 also works for starts-at-1-in-row-2.

questions.q: Copy VALUES only (not formulas) from A1:A10 to B1:B10:
questions.explanation: Cmd+Ctrl+V (Mac) / Ctrl+Alt+V (PC) opens Paste Special. Options: Values, Formulas, Formats, Transpose, etc.

questions.q: Freeze Panes is used for:
choices: Keeping header rows/columns visible while scrolling
questions.explanation: View tab → Freeze Panes. Options: Top Row, First Column, or Panes at cursor position.

questions.q: Cell shows #DIV/0!. Cause:
choices: Divide by zero or blank cell
questions.explanation: Fix with =IFERROR(a/b, 0) or guard with =IF(b=0, 0, a/b).

questions.q: Cell shows #NAME?. Cause:
choices: Misspelled function or undefined named range
questions.explanation: Typos like =SUMM, unquoted text in COUNTIF, or undefined named ranges.

questions.q: Cell shows #REF!. Cause:
choices: A reference is no longer valid (deleted column/row/sheet)
questions.explanation: Broken reference from deleting something the formula depended on.

questions.q: Cell shows #VALUE!. Cause:
choices: Type mismatch — formula expects number, got text (or vice versa)
questions.explanation: =A1+B1 where A1 is text. Common with imported data that looks numeric but is stored as text.

questions.q: VLOOKUP returns #N/A. Cause:
choices: Lookup value not found in lookup column
questions.explanation: "Not Available" = lookup failed. Wrap with IFERROR(VLOOKUP(...), "Not Found") or use XLOOKUP.

questions.q: Wrap a formula to show a custom message on any error:
questions.explanation: IFERROR catches all error types. IFNA catches only #N/A specifically.

questions.q: =IFERROR(A1/B1, 0) does what?
choices: Normal A1/B1, returns 0 on any error
questions.explanation: Evaluates formula. If error, returns fallback. Essential for clean dashboards.

questions.q: You named cell $C$2 as "StateRate". Which formula is valid?
questions.explanation: Named ranges: bare name, no quotes or @. Define via Formulas → Define Name or type in Name Box. Makes formulas self-documenting.

questions.q: The correct VLOOKUP syntax is:
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP(what_to_find, where_to_look, which_column, exact_or_approx). The lookup value must be in the FIRST column of the table_array.

questions.q: In VLOOKUP, the fourth argument (range_lookup) should be FALSE or 0 when:
questions.explanation: FALSE/0 = exact match (use 99% of the time). TRUE/1 = approximate match, requires sorted data.

questions.q: =VLOOKUP("Metro", B2:D50, 3, FALSE) returns:
choices: The value in column C where B column = "Metro"
The value in column D where B column = "Metro"
The third row of the table
An error because Metro isn't sorted
questions.explanation: col_index_num = 3 means the 3rd column of the range B:D, which is D.

questions.q: Why does VLOOKUP FAIL when you need to look up a value and return something from a column to the LEFT of the lookup column?
choices: It doesn't fail, VLOOKUP works in any direction
VLOOKUP only searches right of the first column — use INDEX/MATCH or XLOOKUP instead
You need to sort the data
questions.explanation: VLOOKUP only returns values from columns to the RIGHT of the lookup column. XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH work in any direction.

questions.q: The XLOOKUP syntax is:
questions.explanation: XLOOKUP takes lookup_value, the range to search IN, the range to return FROM. Way cleaner than VLOOKUP.

questions.q: A key advantage of XLOOKUP over VLOOKUP:
choices: Works in both directions (left OR right) and doesn't need column indices
questions.explanation: XLOOKUP works regardless of direction, has built-in not-found handling, and doesn't break if columns are inserted/deleted.

questions.q: =XLOOKUP("King", A:A, C:C, "Not found") does what if "King" isn't in column A?
questions.explanation: The 4th arg is the fallback when no match. VLOOKUP requires IFERROR wrapper to achieve the same.

questions.q: INDEX/MATCH combination is traditionally used because:
choices: It works bidirectionally (unlike VLOOKUP) and survives column inserts
questions.explanation: =INDEX(return_range, MATCH(lookup_value, lookup_range, 0)). Both INDEX/MATCH and XLOOKUP solve VLOOKUP's directional limitation.

questions.q: =IF(A1>=60, "Pass", "Fail") returns:
questions.explanation: IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false). Text values in quotes.

questions.q: Nested IF for letter grades (90+=A, 80+=B, 70+=C, else F):
questions.explanation: Nested IFs go from HIGHEST condition first. Each false branch becomes the next IF.

questions.q: Order matters in nested IF. Which is WRONG?
questions.explanation: Nested IF stops at first TRUE. Low thresholds first = everyone above 70 shows "C" and never reaches the higher grades. Always check highest threshold first.

questions.q: =AND(A1>50, B1<100) returns:
choices: TRUE if either condition is true
TRUE only if BOTH conditions are true
The sum of A1 and B1
questions.explanation: AND requires ALL conditions TRUE. OR requires ANY condition TRUE. NOT inverts.

questions.q: =OR(A1="Metro", A1="Urban") returns:
choices: TRUE if A1 equals either "Metro" OR "Urban"
The longer of the two strings
questions.explanation: OR = at least one is TRUE. Useful for 'does this match any of N categories'.

questions.q: =IF(AND(A1>50, B1<100), "Yes", "No") returns "Yes" when:
questions.explanation: Combine IF with AND: only TRUE branch runs when all AND conditions are met.

questions.q: =NOT(A1="Metro") returns:
choices: TRUE if A1 does NOT equal "Metro"
questions.explanation: NOT inverts: TRUE becomes FALSE, FALSE becomes TRUE.

choices: Excel 2019+ replacement for nested IFs — cleaner syntax
questions.explanation: IFS evaluates pairs in order. Use TRUE as the final catch-all. Much cleaner than deep nesting.

questions.q: To create a chart, you typically:
choices: Type the data and Excel auto-creates a chart
Select the data range, go to Insert tab, pick a chart type
questions.explanation: Select data → Insert → choose chart from the Charts group.

questions.q: For comparing DISCRETE CATEGORIES (populations of different counties), the best chart type is:
questions.explanation: Column/bar charts compare values across categories. Pie = parts of a whole. Line = trends over time.

questions.q: For showing a TREND OVER TIME (population year by year), the best chart is:
questions.explanation: Line charts are designed for continuous data over intervals, especially time.

questions.q: For showing how categories make up a WHOLE (region shares of state population), the best chart is:
questions.explanation: Pie chart = parts of a whole, typically works best with 5 or fewer slices.

questions.q: For showing the RELATIONSHIP between two numeric variables (poverty % vs unemployment rate), the best chart is:
questions.explanation: Scatter = correlation between two numeric variables. Each point is one observation.

questions.q: To change a chart from column to line after creating it:
choices: Right-click the chart → Change Chart Type
questions.explanation: Change Chart Type dialog lets you switch freely without rebuilding.

questions.q: Chart titles, axis labels, and legends are added via:
choices: The Chart Design tab (appears when chart selected) → Add Chart Element
questions.explanation: Chart Design → Add Chart Element → Chart Title / Axis Titles / Legend / Data Labels / etc.

questions.q: A pie chart with 20 tiny slices is typically a problem because:
choices: Pie charts don't support that many values
It's hard to read — too many slices with similar sizes blur together
Pie charts aren't on the Insert tab
questions.explanation: Best practice: pie charts work well with 2-5 slices. More = use column chart.

questions.q: Conditional Formatting is found under:
questions.explanation: Home → Conditional Formatting. Rules, data bars, color scales, icon sets all live here.

questions.q: To highlight all cells in a column greater than 10,000:
choices: Conditional Formatting → Highlight Cells Rules → Greater Than → enter 10000
questions.explanation: Highlight Cells Rules has presets for >, <, between, equal to, text contains, etc.

questions.q: A 'data bar' conditional format:
choices: Draws a horizontal bar inside the cell proportional to its value
questions.explanation: Data bars visualize magnitude within the cell itself — like a mini bar chart per row.

questions.q: To highlight the TOP 10 values in a column automatically:
choices: Conditional Formatting → Top/Bottom Rules → Top 10 Items
questions.explanation: Top/Bottom Rules has presets for Top N, Bottom N, Above/Below Average, etc. Configurable number.

questions.q: A 3-color scale conditional format:
choices: Applies a gradient from low-to-mid-to-high value automatically
Is the same as data bars
questions.explanation: Color Scales grade cells on a red-yellow-green (or other) gradient. Great for heatmaps.

questions.q: =LEFT("Washington", 4) returns:
questions.explanation: LEFT(text, num_chars) — extracts from the left. 4 chars from 'Washington' = 'Wash'.

questions.q: =RIGHT("County-101", 3) returns:
questions.explanation: RIGHT(text, num_chars) — extracts from the right. 3 chars = '101'.

questions.q: =MID("Metro-King-50", 7, 4) returns:
questions.explanation: MID(text, start_num, num_chars) — start at position 7, take 4 characters. 'M-e-t-r-o---K-i-n-g' → position 7 is K, 4 chars = 'King'.

questions.q: =LEN("King County") returns:
questions.explanation: LEN counts all characters including spaces. 'King County' = 4 + 1 + 6 = 11.

questions.q: =TRIM("  King  County  ") returns:
questions.explanation: TRIM removes leading/trailing spaces AND collapses multiple internal spaces to single spaces.

questions.q: =UPPER("washington"), =LOWER("WASHINGTON"), =PROPER("washington") return:
questions.explanation: UPPER → all caps. LOWER → all lowercase. PROPER → first letter of each word capitalized.

questions.q: =A1 & " - " & B1 where A1="King" and B1="Metro" returns:
questions.explanation: & is the concatenation operator. Joins literal strings (in quotes) with cell references.

questions.q: #DIV/0! appears when:
choices: You divide by zero or an empty cell
A value is not found in a lookup
questions.explanation: Division by zero. Common fix: =IFERROR(A1/B1, 0) or =IF(B1=0, 0, A1/B1).

questions.q: #REF! means:
choices: A formula refers to a cell that no longer exists (e.g. deleted row/column)
questions.explanation: Reference error — you deleted a cell that a formula was pointing to.

questions.q: #VALUE! means:
choices: Wrong data type (text where number expected, etc.)
questions.explanation: Type mismatch. E.g. ="abc"*5 or SUM on a range with unexpected text.

questions.q: #N/A in a VLOOKUP usually means:
questions.explanation: Not Available. Wrap in IFERROR or IFNA for graceful handling: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(...), "Not found")

questions.q: #NAME? error typically means:
choices: You typed a function name wrong (e.g. =SUUM) or referenced a named range that doesn't exist
questions.explanation: Excel doesn't recognize the name. Common cause: typo in function name.

questions.q: =IFERROR(VLOOKUP(A1, B:D, 3, FALSE), "Not found") does:
choices: Returns the VLOOKUP result if successful, or "Not found" if the VLOOKUP errors
Returns both the value and the text
questions.explanation: IFERROR(value, value_if_error) — gracefully handles #N/A, #VALUE!, etc.

questions.q: Data Validation is accessed via:
questions.explanation: Data → Data Validation. Restricts allowed values: list (dropdown), whole number, decimal, date, text length, custom formula.

questions.q: To create a dropdown list in a cell limited to values "Metro" and "Non-Metro":
choices: Data → Data Validation → Allow: List → Source: Metro,Non-Metro
questions.explanation: Data Validation with 'List' type. Source can be typed values comma-separated or a cell range.

questions.q: A Washington state pivot with Region in Rows and Count of County in Values shows South Puget Sound. How do you find how many counties are in that region?
choices: Count the rows of the pivot
Look at the value in the Count of County column for the South Puget Sound row
questions.explanation: Pivot tables show the answer directly. Find the row label, read the value.

questions.q: A pivot has Region in Rows, Metro/Non-Metro in Columns, Count of County in Values. To find how many Metro counties are in the Northeast region:
choices: Find the cell at the intersection of Northeast row and Metro column
questions.explanation: Matrix pivots: find intersection of row + column. Cell at (Northeast, Metro) gives the count.

questions.q: A pivot has Region in Rows and Average of Unemployment Rate in Values. To find which region has the HIGHEST average unemployment:
choices: Scan the Average column, identify the LARGEST value, read its region label
questions.explanation: Scan the value column for the largest number. Read the row label for that value.

questions.q: A pivot currently shows Sum of Population but you need Average. How?
choices: Right-click a value cell → Summarize Values By → Average
questions.explanation: Right-click → Summarize Values By → pick Average. Or drag the field setting.

questions.q: Washington state has 39 counties. A pivot with Region in Rows shows counts summing to 39. This confirms:
choices: The pivot captured every county exactly once
questions.explanation: Grand total in a Count pivot = total record count. If it matches the known 39, your pivot is complete.

questions.q: The 'County Growth' rate column calculation uses population growth between 2017 and 2018. The most likely formula is:
questions.explanation: Growth rate = (new - old) / old. Always divide by the starting/old value.

questions.q: For the 'Individual 2019 Population' column using each county's OWN growth rate from column G (not the state-wide $C$2), the formula in H5 should be:
questions.explanation: Use the county's own growth rate G5 (relative — changes per row). Not the state-wide $C$2.

questions.q: The 'Simple 2019' column uses the state growth rate in C2 (1.5%), applied to every county. Formula in G5:
choices: Any of the absolute-reference versions works
questions.explanation: Since C2 must NOT move when dragged down, lock at least the row. $C$2, C$2 both work for column drag.
